extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media researchers, and the informed public interested in Project Veritas and media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging undercover sting operations, deceptive-editing videos, source/document authentication, funding transparency, and whether an actor qualifies as news media for legal/First Amendment protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: News media classification (DOJ 'News Media Policy Consultation' factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Justice Manual does not directly define who qualifies as news media, instead favoring a case-by-case approach using a 'News Media Policy Consultation' form that lays out twelve factors for law enforcement agents to consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate whether individuals or organizations can invoke media/First Amendment protections; example factors explicitly mentioned include whether the individual possesses press credentials and whether they 'primarily [report] facts, as opposed to expressing opinion'. In the Project Veritas case, prosecutors determined O'Keefe didn't meet the department's standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession of press credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the individual possesses press credentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of the factors law enforcement considers when deciding whether a person qualifies as news media for purposes of legal protections; presence or absence of credentials can weigh on that determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primarily reporting facts vs. expressing opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the individual or organization 'primarily [report] facts, as opposed to expressing opinion'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A component of the DOJ's assessment of media status. Organizations whose output is largely opinionated may be less likely to be treated as news media for purposes of certain protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication/verification of documents and sources before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify and authenticate documents and source material before publishing (e.g., Project Veritas chose not to publish Ashley Biden's diary because it could not be authenticated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to authenticate can lead to refusal to publish, legal exposure, reputational damage, and inaccurate reporting; publishers should attempt to corroborate provenance and authenticity before wide dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: VAERS data limitations and appropriate interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: VAERS was designed for purposes of early warning and it may contain 'incomplete, inaccurate, coincidental, or unverifiable' information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims based on VAERS should acknowledge these limitations; despite issues, VAERS can still be helpful to regulators (CDC, FDA) as an early-warning tool. Anti-pattern: treating raw VAERS counts as definitive evidence of causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptive editing (no misleading splicing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial manipulations such as splicing unrelated moments or deceptively editing video/audio to change meaning are deceptive (e.g., splicing Shiller's response was described as 'a blatant deception through editing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deceptive editing undermines credibility and can be described as fabrication; ethical journalism requires contextual and unmanipulated presentation of clips and clear labeling of any edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing quality: avoid thinly-sourced, anonymous, or vague allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from relying on thinly-sourced, anonymous, or vaguely-specified allegations (the article describes some Project Veritas output as 'thinly-sourced and outright implausible' or relying on 'anonymous sources and vague allegations').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust corroboration and transparency about sources strengthens credibility; thin or anonymous sourcing increases risk of error, legal exposure, and inability for others to evaluate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical acceptability of undercover sting tactics / good-faith standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of undercover techniques and sting operations raises ethical questions, particularly when done in 'bad faith'; critics argued Project Veritas 'operates in bad faith' and that some activities 'might not be journalism at all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undercover methods require strong public-interest justification, avoidance of entrapment or fabrication, and adherence to ethical editorial standards. Bad-faith operations (designed to mislead an ideological audience) are an anti-pattern and weaken claims to journalistic legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and provenance of funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose sources of funding and be transparent about major donors (page notes much funding comes from anonymous donations through Donors Trust and lists specific contributions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opaque or donor-advised funding (especially from politically-aligned donors) can signal conflicts of interest or agenda-setting; reporting organizations should disclose major funding to allow evaluation of potential bias or influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdfunding patterns for alleged whistleblowers
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern where supposed whistleblowers rapidly establish crowdfunding pages hyped by the outlet within hours or days of going public (The Daily Dot reported seven examples raising thousands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such temporal patterns can indicate coordinated monetization or question the independence/authenticity of whistleblowers; scrutiny advised when crowdfunding appears immediately and is promoted by the reporting outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-enforcement standards for searches affecting journalists and privileged materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Law enforcement should have good reason to believe reporters were directly involved in criminal activity before subjecting them to invasive searches; appointing a special master can protect attorney-client privilege and First Amendment rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocacy groups (ACLU, Committee to Protect Journalists) argued that, absent a clear link to criminal conduct, raids risk setting a dangerous precedent and that courts should use mechanisms (special master) to constrain law-enforcement access to privileged or irrelevant materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spreading false or implausible conspiracy claims without robust evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims such as rampant voter fraud or backdating ballots were criticized as implausible and thinly sourced (e.g., PV's claims about Michigan USPS workers or other election fraud assertions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence; outlets should avoid amplifying conspiracy theories without verifiable documentation and reputable corroboration, and should correct or retract when evidence is lacking.
